title: POC Weekly Sync - Throughput Optimization
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on throughput improvements. Reviewed benchmark results from last week, discussed continuous batching benefits, concurrency targets, and request queueing behavior. Identified config tweaks (batch window, max concurrency, KV cache priming) to run before next check-in. Agreed to run a 24h load test aim at 1.5x expected production throughput and to share updated benchmark spreadsheet and logs.
action_items: Priya Nair - tweak batch window and sampling policy, run 24h test (due 2026-04-02)
Marcus Lee - provide traffic shape and 7-day tail latency percentiles (due 2026-03-31)
Jordan Hayes - share updated benchmark spreadsheet and upload logs to shared drive (due 2026-03-31)
Alex Romero - confirm pilot SLA acceptance criteria and cost targets (due 2026-04-06)
next_steps: Run 24-hour continuous load test at 1.5x expected production RPS
Share updated benchmark spreadsheet and raw logs
SE to provide recommended batch window and concurrency settings for Dedicated pool
Schedule follow-up check-in in one week (2026-04-06)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 10:00 AM UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Malik Chen (Redwood), Alex Romero (CTO, NovaPay), Priya Singh (Platform Eng, NovaPay), Marcus Lee (ML Infra), Sofia Park (PM)

[00:00] Jordan Hayes: Hey everyone, uh thanks for joining today's weekly POC sync. I think we have a pretty tight agenda today focused on throughput and the tuning changes Priya pushed last week. Quick roll call — Alex, you there?
[00:12] Alex Romero: Yep, here, thanks Jordan. Morning all.
[00:15] Priya Singh: Here.
[00:17] Marcus Lee: Marcus here.
[00:19] Jordan Hayes: Great. Malik and Priya from our side as well. Quick note — we updated the benchmark spreadsheet, I've put a link in the chat, please take a look after the call.
[00:28] Priya Nair: Awesome. So just to recap real quick, last week we changed the batch window from 20ms to 40ms and enabled continuous batching across the Dedicated pool, and we also increased the max concurrency per worker by two to try to hit higher throughput. Results were mixed — we saw throughput up about 22% on average but tail latency moved up slightly during spikes.
[00:45] Marcus Lee: Yeah we saw that in our logs. The p95 jumped from ~180ms to 240ms on some bursts, p99 was a bit noisier. But the average token latencies improved, so it's a tradeoff.
[00:58] Priya Singh: Is that with KV priming disabled? I remember we had two runs — one where the KV cache hit rate was low and one where we primed it.
[01:07] Priya Nair: Correct, the main benchmark I'm talking about was without explicit priming; it's the default cold start for most sequences. The primed run showed much better p95, around 190ms, and throughput stayed high. The trade is the warm-up period.
[01:20] Alex Romero: Can you explain quickly the difference between continuous batching and our previous setup? Our infra team wants to make sure we understand the queuing behavior.
[01:27] Priya Nair: Sure. Previously we were doing micro-batching with an immediate dispatch — so small batches every X ms but not aggregating across workers. Continuous batching lets the runtime accumulate requests across the GPU's dispatch window and across in-flight tokens, so you get larger effective batch sizes which improve GPU utilization. The downside is slightly more queueing at the scheduler level which can raise tail latencies if concurrency spikes.
[01:46] Jordan Hayes: In practice that means you get better tokens/sec and lower cost per token but you may need to tune concurrency ceilings and queue thresholds to preserve p99 SLAs.
[01:56] Marcus Lee: Right, so if we set batch window too high we risk increasing user-facing latency for our interactive flows. We care about median <120ms and p95 <250ms for the critical path.
[02:07] Malik Chen: That's helpful. One thing we didn't show in the spreadsheet is the queue length distribution. During the 40ms run there were short spikes to queue length 7-9 which corresponded to the p99 blips. We're thinking about adding a max_queue_size setting and an overflow policy — either drop to a cheaper fallback model or route to a lower-capacity worker.
[02:27] Priya Singh: Routing to fallback — is that already supported in the POC? We need to make sure data residency and logging are preserved when we failover.
[02:34] Priya Nair: Yes, smart routing and fallback policies are supported. For the pilot we've been simulating a fallback to the hosted smaller model variant in the same region, and logs/trace IDs flow through the control plane so you keep observability. We'll, uh, confirm the exact retention you need.
[02:47] Alex Romero: Okay good. Cost is big for us — what kind of cost delta are we expecting with continuous batching on Dedicated vs our current internal infra?
[02:56] Jordan Hayes: Early numbers show ~18-25% lower per-token cost due to better GPU packing. That depends on your workload shape — more short bursts reduces the benefit. We'll send a cost breakdown tied to the benchmark runs.
[03:08] Marcus Lee: For the 24h test can we run a traffic shape that mirrors our weekend peak and also a synthetic steady-state? The weekend peak has lots of small requests interleaved with longer ones, it's cause of the worst tails.
[03:19] Priya Nair: Absolutely, Marcus — if you can upload the 5-minute resolution traffic shape and a couple of sample request payloads to the shared drive that'd help. We can run both the weekend-shaped run and a steady RPS run at 1.5x prod.
[03:33] Alex Romero: We'll get that to you by tomorrow.
[03:36] Sofia Park: Quick product question — are we losing any of our function-calling guarantees with batching? e.g., ordering or determinism?
[03:43] Malik Chen: Good question. Function/tool calling order is preserved per-request; batching doesn't change inherent ordering guarantees for a single connection. However, if you route to fallback models, you might observe small divergence in outputs which is typical. We log all inputs and outputs so you can reconcile.
[03:56] Priya Singh: Another item — our security team asked about KMS integration for Dedicated. We saw from the doc that you support customer-managed keys but wanted to confirm whether rotation makes any inference outage windows.
[04:07] Priya Nair: We support KMS/HSM and key rotation with zero-downtime — keys are cached at the control plane with short-lived tokens, rotation is seamless for inference. We'll share the SOC2/ISO and KMS integration notes after the call.
[04:20] Jordan Hayes: Cool. Back to tuning — Priya, what are your recommended next config changes based on the last run?
[04:25] Priya Nair: I'd recommend three immediate changes: lower the batch window to 30ms (midpoint), cap worker concurrency at current+1 instead of +2, and enable KV priming for the top 15% most common prompt prefixes during warm-up. That should keep throughput gains while reducing p95 variability.
[04:39] Marcus Lee: If we cap concurrency won't that reduce throughput some?
[04:42] Priya Nair: Slightly, but in our sims we see throughput drop only 6-8% while p95 improves by ~12-15% on bursty shapes. It's a better balance for your SLA targets.
[04:54] Alex Romero: Can you also quantify the effect on cost? If throughput drops 8% we'd expect cost/wall-clock to increase, but cost/token might stay similar. We need the number for the procurement folks.
[05:05] Jordan Hayes: We'll compute cost-per-token and cost-per-sec for both settings and include it in the spreadsheet.
[05:11] Priya Singh: For the KV cache priming — how do you determine top prefixes? Are you sampling logs or do we provide a seed set?
[05:18] Priya Nair: We can do both. Marcus can drop an S3 with a week of requests and we run a frequency analysis to pick the top ~5K prefixes to prime. Alternatively, you can provide an authoritative list if you prefer.
[05:29] Marcus Lee: We'll share the logs. Note they contain PII so we'll redact prior to upload; we can provide an anonymized prefix file.
[05:36] Jordan Hayes: Great. Any other blockers?
[05:39] Sofia Park: I just want to confirm the timeline — we want to decide on Dedicated config by next Wednesday to align with budget cycle.
[05:46] Jordan Hayes: Understood. Our plan: run the 24h tests this week, update spreadsheet and logs by Wednesday, and then meet next Tuesday/Wednesday to lock configs.
[05:56] Alex Romero: Sounds good. One more technical detail — queues and preemptive scheduling. If there is a sudden spike, can Redwood preempt long running requests to free GPU for short interactive ones?
[06:08] Priya Nair: We support preemptible work units in the scheduler for certain model families; you can configure preemption policies per-route. There's a slight overhead for state checkpointing but it's small. We'll show an example in the next run.
[06:20] Marcus Lee: Great. Please also capture the worker-level telemetry, not just control-plane timing — we want to see GPU kernel utilization and dispatch gaps.
[06:28] Malik Chen: We already capture those metrics. We'll attach GPU flame graphs and the dispatch histograms to the logs bundle.
[06:34] Jordan Hayes: Ok let's recap next steps and owners. Priya N to run the 24h with updated settings (30ms window, +1 concurrency cap, KV priming top prefixes). Marcus to upload traffic shapes and anonymized logs. Jordan to post updated spreadsheet and cost calc. Alex to confirm SLA targets and procurement thresholds.
[06:52] Alex Romero: Yep, I'll follow up with procurement and get back on the cost targets.
[06:56] Priya Singh: One small ask — can we get a short runbook for emergency fallback routing in case of regional capacity issues?
[07:02] Jordan Hayes: Yes we'll attach a one-page runbook and the playbook for failover to hosted variants.
[07:08] Malik Chen: I'll also add a note on debug flags to enable verbose tracing for a limited window so you can correlate traces.
[07:15] Sofia Park: Thanks everyone.
[07:17] Jordan Hayes: Thanks all. We'll send notes and action items. Next check-in same time next week?
[07:21] Alex Romero: Works for me.
[07:23] Priya Singh: Works.
[07:25] Jordan Hayes: Great. End call.

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription errors typical of auto-transcribe (names, acronyms). Links shared during call: benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/novapay-poc-benchmarks), logs upload folder (s3://novapay-poc/logs/2026-03-30), security docs (link: https://redwood.example.com/docs/security), runbook doc (link: https://redwood.example.com/docs/novapay-runbook).
